R3_tool_decision_quality.rationale: A stated, case-specific need: declared imports are needed to see FS manipulation APIs, and the initial evidence lacked them.

R4_new_evidence_relevance.rationale: Clearly relevant. Visible entries include fread, fwrite and feof (file-stream I/O). Committed entries add _mkdir, _tempnam, _stat, _unlink, _open/_read/_write/_close, remove, fopen and fclose.

R5_new_evidence_consumption.rationale: The new evidence is misread. The report lists fread and fwrite among the visible imports but calls them 'standard runtime functions' and concludes there are 'no explicit file-system APIs in the first 16 entries'. These are file read/write functions directly relevant to the question. Reachable committed entries (_unlink, _mkdir, remove, fopen at 18-40) were left unread without saying they were reachable. The access_limits note says committed-but-unseen entries were reachable only by bounded page reads (at most 2 x 16), and the material does not show whether that read action was offered here.

R6_incremental_value.rationale: Net misleading. The report tells an analyst that no file-system APIs are visible when visible fread, fwrite and feof show declared file read/write capability. It also frames the recommendation around a 'strong benign signal'. An analyst relying on it would wrongly conclude the visible imports show no FS capability.

claims.rationale: The visible entries include fread (12), feof (13) and fwrite (15), which are file-stream read/write functions. Saying there are no explicit file-system APIs in the first 16 contradicts what the author saw.
16 of 64 committed visible. The absence caveat is correct.
